concepts.name: Module resolution models the runtime host

questions.prompt: A TypeScript file contains a top-level export. What does that establish about its ordinary top-level declarations?

choices.text: They belong to the module scope rather than the shared script global scope.
They become globally visible to every script without any explicit import.
They are copied into every importing file as independently mutable globals.
They disappear from runtime code even when they are exported values.

questions.explanation: A top-level import or export makes a module. Its declarations are scoped to that module and exported bindings require appropriate imports.

sources.title: TypeScript: Modules
sources.claim: Files with top-level imports or exports are modules with their own scope; dynamic import is asynchronous and type-only imports disappear.

questions.prompt: A file uses `import type {User} from "./types"`. What happens to that import in emitted JavaScript?

choices.text: It eagerly runs the imported module to validate every User instance.
It becomes a fetch call that downloads a runtime interface object.
It creates a runtime User constructor from the imported type definition.
It is erased because it supplies types rather than runtime values.

questions.explanation: Type-only imports are removed. They do not import runtime values or generate constructors and validation.

questions.prompt: A Node project emits one module format while configuring resolution assumptions for an unrelated host. What should be reviewed?

choices.text: Switch every import to any so the runtime can infer the intended module format.
Assume moduleResolution alone changes Node into a browser bundler host.
Align TypeScript resolution and emitted module assumptions with the actual runtime host.
Assume type-check success guarantees every emitted import resolves at runtime.

questions.explanation: TypeScript models a host resolution strategy; the runtime ultimately loads emitted modules. Correct checking requires matching the host assumptions rather than treating compiler options as runtime changes.

questions.prompt: Code uses `import("./feature")` in an async loading path. What is the loading contract?

choices.text: It guarantees the module is not evaluated until an export is first read.
It returns a promise for the module namespace when loading succeeds.
It synchronously returns the namespace before any loading work can occur.
It returns only the TypeScript type declarations and no runtime values.

questions.explanation: Dynamic import is asynchronous and yields the module namespace through a promise. It is not a type-only import or a lazy-per-export evaluation guarantee.

questions.prompt: A file has no imports or exports and is treated as a script in the stated compiler configuration. Why might its top-level name conflict with another script?

choices.text: Script declarations can share global scope across files.
Script declarations automatically get one isolated scope per filename.
Every script file receives a generated namespace matching its folder.
Every top-level script declaration is erased before global names are checked.

questions.explanation: A script can contribute to global scope. Module scope is different, and the question explicitly states the file is classified as a script.

questions.prompt: A symbol imported with import type is needed by a runtime expression. What is the issue?

choices.text: The import automatically changes into a value import when execution starts.
The runtime synthesizes an object from the static type name on first use.
The expression works because all TypeScript types exist as runtime values.
A type-only import cannot provide a runtime value for that expression.

questions.explanation: Type-only imports are erased and cannot supply a value. A value import is needed for runtime use of a value-exported symbol.

questions.prompt: A codebase mixes script files and ES modules. Which scope claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Top-level imports or exports establish a module.
Module declarations have their own scope.
Every exported value is automatically global in every browser script.
Script files can contribute declarations to global scope.
A filename alone creates an ES module namespace in every host.

questions.explanation: a: They distinguish module files in the described model. b: They do not automatically populate shared script globals. c: Consumers use imports rather than automatic global visibility. d: Scripts can share that scope when classified as scripts. e: Module classification depends on syntax and host or compiler configuration.

questions.prompt: A build uses explicit type-only imports. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It cannot provide a runtime value for an expression.
It automatically executes the module for side effects.
It generates runtime validators for imported interfaces.
It guarantees a runtime constructor exists for each imported interface.
import type is erased from emitted JavaScript.

questions.explanation: a: No value import remains after erasure. b: Its erasure removes that runtime import. c: Imported types do not turn into validation code. d: An interface need not have any runtime value. e: It supplies only type information.

questions.prompt: A package must run in a specific host. Which configuration claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Type lookup may find declarations rather than implementation code.
Changing a compiler option rewrites the host own resolver automatically.
A resolved declaration file alone proves an implementation exists at runtime.
The host determines actual module loading behavior.
TypeScript resolution should model that host.

questions.explanation: a: TypeScript can resolve supporting types while the host loads JavaScript. b: The host still follows its runtime rules. c: Type availability and runtime loadability are different checks. d: The emitted code is interpreted by its runtime host. e: The compiler must predict the host lookup behavior.

questions.prompt: A team reviews asynchronous module loading. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Dynamic import always returns synchronously without a promise.
Type-only imports perform the same runtime loading as dynamic import.
Dynamic import returns a promise for the namespace.
The application must handle possible load failure.
A declaration file is a substitute for the runtime implementation.

questions.explanation: a: It is the asynchronous import expression. b: Type-only imports are erased. c: Loading and evaluation are represented asynchronously. d: The returned promise can reject. e: Declarations provide types rather than executable implementation.
